{"id": "a5c3aa95a9024b2995bcfdf81fa45cae", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The spikes in VolumeQueueLength and write latency on gp3 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 (attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_6 as /dev/sdf) come from a fault-injection test. They are not caused by a shortage of IOPS or throughput. AWS FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7, built from template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 and using role example-fis, started at 19:32:35Z. Its aws:ebs:volume-io-latency action has been running since 19:32:46Z and targets only this volume. It adds 500 ms to 100% of write I/O and 50% of read I/O, it lasts PT60M (so it should end around 20:32Z), and it has no stop condition. Each I/O now takes longer, so outstanding I/Os pile up in the queue and the number of completed operations drops. The workload itself has not grown: it is a steady ~1,000 IOPS (500 read + 500 write), a third of the 3,000 IOPS provisioned. Adding IOPS or throughput would not help, because the extra latency is injected per I/O whatever the provisioned performance. The same template already ran at 18:45Z (EXP1234567890abcdef_6, later stopped by a user), and the same pattern of queue spike plus latency appeared at 18:46–18:56Z. To resolve this, stop experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 or let it finish. Adding a CloudWatch alarm as a stop condition to the template would also help.
## Evidence
- FIS get_experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7: status running, started 2026-11-23T19:32:35Z. Action aws:ebs:volume-io-latency started 19:32:46Z on target vol-0123456789abcdef0, with writeIOLatencyMilliseconds=500, writeIOPercentage=100, readIOLatencyMilliseconds=500, readIOPercentage=50, duration=PT60M, stopConditions=none.
- FIS list_experiments: earlier run EXP1234567890abcdef_6 of the same template was created at 18:45:16Z and later stopped by a user. It lines up with the earlier queue spike.
- CloudWatch AWS/EBS VolumeQueueLength (5-min average): baseline 0.77; 15.5–16.0 at 18:46–18:56Z (first experiment); 8.4 in the 19:31Z bucket (current experiment).
- Average write latency (VolumeTotalWriteTime ÷ VolumeWriteOps): baseline ~0.95 ms (143 s / 150,002 ops); ~275 ms at 18:46Z; ~504 ms at 18:51Z; ~21.6 ms across the whole 19:31Z bucket, which only partly overlaps the experiment.
- Baseline load from VolumeWriteOps and VolumeReadOps: ~150,000 each per 5 min, so ~1,000 total IOPS against 3,000 provisioned. During injection, ops fell (to 6–11k per 5 min) rather than rising, which means the volume was not saturated.
- EC2 describe_volumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is gp3, 20 GiB, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s, tagged Name=example-d-gp3-fis.
- VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no datapoints in the window, so there is no sign the provisioned limits were exceeded.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0
- i-1234567890abcdef0_6
- [redacted ARN]
- FIS template EXT1234567890abcdef_5
## Gaps
- I did not pull the CloudTrail StartExperiment event, so I have not identified which principal started the current experiment.
- Application-level write latency was not checked directly; it is inferred from the EBS volume metrics.
- The IOPS/throughput exceeded checks had no datapoints, possibly because they are not emitted for this instance type. The ops counts alone show the volume running well below its provisioned IOPS.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

I've now pinpointed the root cause: FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7, launched by Admin/example-session at 19:32:35 via aws-cli, injected 500ms latency, and since the workload is closed-loop with roughly 16 outstanding I/Os pinned in queue, throughput collapsed from ~1,000 IOPS to ~42 IOPS per Little's law — scaling IOPS won't fix this. Application write latency jumped. The user asked whether to add more IOPS.

Established root cause (ground truth, confirmed — do not re-investigate):
- Mitigation category: Changes (an intentional fault-injection change that is still running).
- AWS FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 ([redacted ARN]), from template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 ([redacted ARN], "example scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency"), role [redacted ARN]. It was started at 2026-11-23T19:32:35Z by [redacted ARN] through aws-cli (CloudTrail StartExperiment). The template was updated 3 seconds earlier (UpdateExperimentTemplate at 19:32:32Z, same principal).
- Action aws:ebs:volume-io-latency has been running since 19:32:46Z against only vol-0123456789abcdef0: writeIOLatencyMilliseconds=500, writeIOPercentage=100, readIOLatencyMilliseconds=500, readIOPercentage=50, duration=PT60M (expected end around 20:32:46Z), stopConditions=[{source: none}]. Status: running.
- Metric evidence: write latency (VolumeTotalWriteTime/VolumeWriteOps) went from a baseline of ~0.95 ms to ~504 ms starting 19:34Z. Read latency went from ~0.59 ms to ~250 ms. VolumeQueueLength went from 0.77 to a flat 15.998. Completed IOPS fell from ~500 write + ~500 read to ~21 + ~21. Baseline demand (~1,000 IOPS, ~16 KiB I/O, ~8 MB/s write) is about a third of the 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s provisioned. Instance EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% are 99%. The other volumes on the instance (vol-1234567890abcdef0_29, vol-1234567890abcdef0_17) are unaffected. Adding IOPS/throughput would not help, because the latency is injected per I/O.
- Prior occurrence: the same template ran as experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_6 at 18:45:16Z (stopped by user). It caused the same queue/latency spike at 18:46–18:56Z, and the alarm went to ALARM at 18:49:48Z and back to OK at 18:59:48Z after the stop.

Actionable causes for mitigation:
1. The running FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 is injecting 500 ms latency into vol-0123456789abcdef0. A bounded fix: stop the experiment (or let it expire at ~20:32Z if the impact is intended/accepted). After stopping, latency should return to ~1 ms and the queue length to ~0.77.
2. Forward-looking: template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 has no stop condition, so nothing halts the injection automatically when the application is impaired. Consider adding a CloudWatch alarm (e.g. example-d-gp3-queue-length or an application latency alarm) as a stop condition, and/or a shorter duration.
Not recommended: modifying the volume's IOPS/throughput (no capacity limit is involved)."}, "type": "tool_use"}], "user_reference": null}

", "signature": "", "type": "thinking"}, {"text": "**No, adding IOPS won't help.** The volume isn't short on capacity. An AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) experiment is deliberately adding 500 ms of delay to every write on vol-0123456789abcdef0, and that delay is added no matter how much IOPS you provision. To recover, stop the experiment or let it end on its own at about **20:32:46Z**.

**What's going on**
- **What caused it:** FIS experiment `EXP1234567890abcdef_7`, from template `EXT1234567890abcdef_5` ("example scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency"), started at 19:32:35Z. CloudTrail shows `assumed-role/Admin/example-session` started it from the aws-cli, three seconds after updating the template. Since 19:32:46Z its `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` action has been adding 500 ms to 100% of writes and 50% of reads on this volume only. It runs for 60 minutes and has no stop condition.
- **How it shows up:**
  - Average write latency went from about 0.95 ms to about 504 ms.
  - Read latency went from about 0.59 ms to about 250 ms.
  - The queue length went from 0.77 to a flat ~16.
  - The 1-minute queue length has been above the alarm threshold of 4 since 19:34Z, which is what fired the alarm.
- **Why the queue grows but throughput drops:** The workload seems to keep a fixed number of requests (about 16) in flight. When each request takes 500 ms, the queue fills to that number and completed operations collapse from about 1,000 IOPS to about 42. If the volume were really saturated, operations would stay at the limit while latency rose. Here they fell.
- **Capacity is not the problem:**
  - Before the experiment, demand was a steady ~500 reads and ~500 writes per second, about a third of the 3,000 IOPS provisioned.
  - Writes were about 8 MB/s against 125 MiB/s provisioned.
  - The instance's EBS I/O and bandwidth balances stayed at 99%, so it isn't being throttled either.
  - The other two volumes on i-1234567890abcdef0_6 show no change.
- **It has happened before:** The same template ran at 18:45:16Z as experiment `EXP1234567890abcdef_6`. It caused the same spike from 18:46 to 18:56Z and the same alarm (ALARM at 18:49:48Z, OK at 18:59:48Z once a user stopped it).

**What to do**
1. **Now:** stop `EXP1234567890abcdef_7` in the FIS console or with `aws fis stop-experiment --id EXP1234567890abcdef_7`. Based on the last run, latency should return to about 1 ms and the alarm should clear within a few minutes. If the impact is part of a planned test, you can instead let it run out at about 20:32:46Z.
2. **Next time:** add a stop condition to `EXT1234567890abcdef_5` so an alarm halts the experiment automatically. That could be `example-d-gp3-queue-length` or an application latency alarm. You could also shorten the duration, and let the team know before running it again.

A mitigation plan with these steps is being prepared separately.

**Not checked:**
- I didn't measure the application's write latency directly; it comes from the volume's CloudWatch metrics.
- I didn't confirm with the person who started it whether this run was intended.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### Write latency and queue-depth spikes on vol-0123456789abcdef0
**Description:** On the gp3 volume, average queue length rose from 0.77 to 16.0. Write latency rose from about 0.95 ms to about 504 ms and read latency from about 0.59 ms to about 250 ms, while read and write IOPS each fell from about 500 to about 21. There were two windows: 18:46–18:56 UTC (the alarm was in ALARM from 18:49:48 to 18:59:48), and from 19:33 UTC, still ongoing (the alarm re-entered ALARM at 19:36:48 UTC). The queue-length alarm also fired earlier the same day, at 07:43, 08:39 and 16:51 UTC.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T18:45:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: FIS experiments are injecting I/O impairment on the volume
**Description:** Both spike windows begin at the start of an experiment from FIS template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 (tagged Project=example). EXP1234567890abcdef_6 was created at 18:45:16 and later stopped by a user; EXP1234567890abcdef_7 was created at 19:32:34 and is still running. Earlier experiments at 07:40, 08:35 and 16:47 line up with earlier alarm transitions (07:43, 08:39, 16:51). The template's actions and targets have not been verified yet.
**Cascades to:** symptom-vol-latency-queue

#### Gaps
- **Application-level latency not measured:** Write latency was measured only from the volume's CloudWatch metrics. Application-side state on i-1234567890abcdef0_6 (retries, backlog, timeouts) and the application's own latency were not checked, so confirm the application recovers after the stop.
- **No data from EBS detailed performance metrics:** VolumeIOPSExceededCheck, VolumeThroughputExceededCheck, VolumeAvgWriteLatency and VolumeStalledIOCheck returned no datapoints for 17:30–19:36 UTC. Write latency was instead calculated from VolumeTotalWriteTime ÷ VolumeWriteOps.

### Root Cause: FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 started with no stop condition
**Description:** Admin/example-session started experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (template EXT1234567890abcdef_5) from the aws-cli at 19:32:35 UTC, 3 s after updating the template. Since 19:32:46 UTC its aws:ebs:volume-io-latency action has added 500 ms to 100% of writes and 50% of reads on vol-0123456789abcdef0 only. It runs for 60 minutes, ending around 20:32:46 UTC, and has no stop condition. The workload keeps about 16 I/Os in flight, so the queue sits at 16 while completed operations fall from about 1,000 to about 42 IOPS. This is not a capacity limit: demand is about a third of the 3,000 provisioned IOPS, and adding IOPS would not remove the injected latency. The same template caused the 18:46–18:56 UTC spike as experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_6.
**Cascades to:** finding-fis-io-impairment, symptom-vol-latency-queue

#### Supporting Observations
- **Running FIS experiment injects 500 ms I/O latency into this volume:** Experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 (template EXT1234567890abcdef_5, 'example scenario d: 500 ms EBS I/O latency') runs as role [redacted ARN]. It targets only [redacted ARN]. Its action aws:ebs:volume-io-latency has parameters writeIOLatencyMilliseconds=500, writeIOPercentage=100, readIOLatencyMilliseconds=500, readIOPercentage=50 and duration=PT60M. The action started at 19:32:46 UTC and is running. There is no stop condition (source: none). The template was last updated at 19:32:32 UTC. A CloudTrail lookup of fis.amazonaws.com write events between 18:30 and 19:37 UTC returned nothing.
- **Admin user changed the FIS template and started the experiment:** CloudTrail shows UpdateExperimentTemplate on EXT1234567890abcdef_5 at 19:32:32 UTC, then StartExperiment at 19:32:35 UTC. Both calls came from [redacted ARN] using aws-cli from Kiro IDE (source IP 67.185.222.142). The experiment template still has no stop condition.
- **Latency step at 19:33 matches the injected values:** At 1-minute resolution, write latency was 0.95 ms and read latency 0.59 ms until 19:32. From 19:34 write latency was about 504 ms and read latency about 250 ms, which is 500 ms on half of reads. Write and read IOPS each fell from 500 to about 21, and queue length rose from 0.77 to 16.0. The instance is a c6i.large (EbsOptimized=false) launched at 18:05 UTC. The alarm uses 60 s periods with 3 of 3 datapoints to alarm.
- **Workload is steady and well below gp3 limits:** Outside the spike windows the volume sustains about 500 read and 500 write IOPS (about 1,000 of 3,000 provisioned) and about 8 MiB/s of writes (125 MiB/s provisioned), with queue length 0.77 and about 0.95 ms latency. During the spikes, IOPS fell and idle time dropped to 0 while latency reached about 504 ms. Throughput did not rise, so this is not an over-limit workload. Burst writes of about 1,089 IOPS at 19:00 reflect a backlog draining.
- **Instance and other attached volumes are unaffected:** On i-1234567890abcdef0_6, EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99% and CPU at 0.5–1.5% between 19:25 and 19:36 UTC. Queue length on the other attached volumes, vol-1234567890abcdef0_29 (/dev/xvda) and vol-1234567890abcdef0_17 (/dev/sdg), stayed at about 0. The impairment is limited to vol-0123456789abcdef0; it is not an instance-level EBS bottleneck.
- **FIS experiment starts line up with every queue-length alarm:** The alarm entered ALARM 3–4 minutes after each experiment from template EXT1234567890abcdef_5 started: 07:40:05 → 07:43:48, 08:35:45 → 08:39:48, 16:47:03 → 16:51:48 and 18:45:16 → 18:49:48. The latest experiment, EXP1234567890abcdef_7 ([redacted ARN]), started at 19:32:34 and is still running; queue length is back at 16.

#### Gaps
- **Not confirmed whether the experiment run was intended:** It was not checked with Admin/example-session whether experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 was a planned test.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Stop the running FIS experiment EXP1234567890abcdef_7 to remove the injected 500 ms I/O latency from vol-0123456789abcdef0. Do not change the volume's IOPS or throughput. As prevention, add a stop condition and a shorter duration to template EXT1234567890abcdef_5.

## Reasoning
The experiment's aws:ebs:volume-io-latency action (PT60M, from 19:32:46 UTC) adds 500 ms to 100% of writes and 50% of reads, and nothing stops it automatically. It will run until about 20:32:46 UTC. Demand (about 1,000 IOPS, about 8 MB/s) is about a third of the 3,000 IOPS / 125 MiB/s provisioned, so extra capacity would not help. After the earlier run EXP1234567890abcdef_6 was stopped, the alarm cleared in about 10 minutes. If the impact is part of a planned test, you can let the experiment expire instead. Note: the automated safety checker rejected this plan three times under a delete/terminate rule. The subagent judged that a false positive, since stopping an experiment deletes nothing. Review before you run it.
